title: Fire, Feast and a Warning
overview: After Solomon's prayer, God shows he accepts the new temple with fire and glory, the nation celebrates for two weeks, and God answers Solomon with both a promise and a warning.

parts.label: Fire and glory (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Fire falling on the offerings was a sign, seen at other key moments in Israel's story, that God accepted them, and the bright cloud of God's presence filled the building so fully that the priests could not go in. The crowd bowed with faces to the ground and sang a familiar refrain: the LORD is good, and his faithful love lasts forever.

parts.label: A dedication feast (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: The huge numbers of animals mark a national event, though some scholars think the figures are rounded or larger than life. Many were fellowship offerings, where most of the meat was eaten by the worshippers, and there were so many that Solomon set apart the middle of the courtyard as extra altar space.

parts.label: Two weeks of celebration (vv. 8-10)
parts.note: People came from the far north of the land to its southern border for seven days dedicating the altar, followed by the seven-day autumn harvest Festival of Shelters. They went home on the twenty-third day of the seventh month, glad about the good God had done for David, Solomon and the whole people.

parts.label: God answers at night (vv. 11-16)
parts.note: God tells Solomon his prayer is heard and the temple chosen as the place where God's Name, meaning his presence, will be. When drought, locusts or disease come, God promises that if the people humble themselves, pray and turn from wrongdoing, he will forgive them and heal their land.

parts.label: A promise to the royal line (vv. 17-18)
parts.note: If Solomon stays faithful as his father David did, his family will keep the throne of Israel. This repeats God's earlier covenant, a binding promise, made to David.

parts.label: A stark warning (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: If the people turn to other gods, they will be uprooted and the temple reduced to rubble, so that passersby are appalled and ask why, and are told it is because the people abandoned the LORD who freed them from Egypt. The book's first readers lived after Babylon destroyed this temple in 586 BC, and the writer presents that disaster as the outcome warned of here.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the promise in verse 14 was given only to ancient Israel and its temple or can be applied today to the church or even to modern nations seeking renewal.
think: When something goes badly wrong for a person or a whole country, how do you decide how much of it to trace back to their own choices?
